rd-school-c6-social-a.ch07-cultural-root.title: India's Cultural Roots
rd-school-c6-social-a.ch07-cultural-root.subtitle: The Vedas, the Upanishads, the Buddha, Mahavira and the folk and tribal wisdom that grew into one great banyan

items.what: Rig Veda hymns composed in the Sapta Sindhu region
Other Vedas, Brahmanas; early Upanishads
Lives of the Buddha and Mahavira
Ashoka supports the spread of Buddhism
Folk and tribal traditions grow alongside, passed on orally

fig.caption: An approximate sequence; exact dates are debated by scholars.

sections.md:
The word **Veda** comes from the Sanskrit root *vid*, 'to know'. The Vedas are a vast collection of hymns, prayers and ritual knowledge composed in an early form of Sanskrit. There are **four Vedas**:

| Veda | Main content |
|---|---|
| **Rig Veda** | Over 1,000 hymns (*suktas*) to deities like Agni (fire), Indra, Varuna, Surya, Ushas (dawn) |
| **Sama Veda** | Melodies (*samans*) for singing hymns; important for the history of Indian music |
| **Yajur Veda** | Formulas and instructions for rituals (*yajnas*) |
| **Atharva Veda** | Hymns for daily life, healing, protection and well-being |

The **Rig Veda** is the oldest; many scholars place its composition broadly in the 2nd millennium BCE, though dates are debated. It was composed mainly in the region of the **Sapta Sindhu** ('land of seven rivers') in north-western India.

**Oral tradition.** For many centuries the Vedas were not written down. They were memorised and passed from teacher to student with astonishing precision using special recitation methods — reciting words forwards, in pairs, and in complex patterns so that a single mistake would be noticed. **UNESCO** has recognised Vedic chanting as part of the world's intangible cultural heritage.

**Ideas in the Vedas.**

- **Rita** — a cosmic order that keeps the universe, seasons and life in balance; this idea later grew into **dharma** (duty, right conduct).
- Respect for **nature** — fire, water, rivers, dawn, earth were honoured.
- Questions about creation: one famous hymn, the *Nasadiya Sukta*, wonders how the universe began and ends by suggesting that perhaps even the highest one does not know — a remarkable spirit of questioning.
- Assemblies called **sabha** and **samiti** where people discussed matters.
- Women composers: some hymns are credited to women seers such as **Lopamudra** and **Ghosha**.

A well-known Rig Vedic thought says, in essence, that truth is one though the wise call it by many names — often seen as a root of Indian acceptance of many views.
keyTerms: Rishi — seer who composed hymns
Yajna — fire ritual
Rita — cosmic order

check.q: How were the Vedas preserved for many centuries?
options: Through precise oral memorisation and recitation
check.why: Teachers and students used careful recitation patterns to pass the Vedas on orally without change.

sections.md:
Later Vedic texts include the **Upanishads**. The word suggests 'sitting near' — students sitting near a teacher to learn deep truths. They are written as conversations and stories.

The Upanishads asked big questions: *Who am I? What is real? What happens after death? What is the source of everything?*

Two key ideas:

- **Brahman** — the ultimate reality, the one essence behind the whole universe.
- **Atman** — the inner self of each being. A central teaching is that the Atman and Brahman are, at the deepest level, one. A famous phrase, *tat tvam asi* ('that thou art'), expresses this.

This means every living being shares the same essence — a basis for treating all with respect.

The Upanishads are full of memorable stories. In one, a student called **Satyakama** honestly tells a teacher he does not know who his father is, and the teacher accepts him for his truthfulness. Women thinkers like **Gargi** and **Maitreyi** appear in debates — Gargi questions the sage Yajnavalkya so sharply in a royal assembly that he warns her not to push further! Ideas of **karma** (actions have consequences) and **rebirth** became widely discussed in this period.

check.q: In the Upanishads, what is the relationship taught between Atman and Brahman?
options: They are at the deepest level one
Atman is a god of fire
check.why: The Upanishads teach that the inner self (Atman) is ultimately one with the universal reality (Brahman).

sections.md:
Over centuries, Indian thinkers developed several systems of philosophy called **darshanas** ('ways of seeing'). Six are often listed together:

| School | Main focus |
|---|---|
| **Nyaya** | Logic and correct reasoning |
| **Vaisheshika** | Nature of matter; atoms (*paramanu*) |
| **Samkhya** | Matter (*prakriti*) and consciousness (*purusha*) |
| **Yoga** | Discipline of body and mind to reach inner freedom |
| **Mimamsa** | Interpreting Vedic ritual and duty |
| **Vedanta** | Interpreting the Upanishads |

There were other schools too, such as the **Charvaka** (or Lokayata), who doubted everything not seen by the senses. Thinkers debated openly; debating was itself a respected art, with rules about fair argument.

**Yoga** is perhaps the best-known gift to the world. The *Yoga Sutras* attributed to **Patanjali** describe an eight-limbed path, including ethical rules, postures (*asanas*), breath control (*pranayama*) and meditation. Since 2015, **21 June** is celebrated worldwide as **International Day of Yoga**.

check.q: Which school of philosophy focused mainly on logic and correct reasoning?
check.why: Nyaya developed careful rules of logic and debate for reaching correct knowledge.

sections.md:
Around the 6th–5th century BCE (scholars debate the exact dates), many new thinkers questioned ritual and searched for new answers. Among them was **Siddhartha Gautama**, a prince of the **Shakya** clan, born at **Lumbini** (in present-day Nepal).

Tradition says that on seeing an old man, a sick man, a dead body and a calm ascetic, he realised that all life involves suffering and change. He left his palace to seek the truth. After years of searching, he meditated under a **peepal tree** at **Bodh Gaya** (Bihar) and attained **enlightenment** — he became the **Buddha**, 'the awakened one'. That tree's descendant is called the **Bodhi tree**.

He gave his **first sermon** at **Sarnath** near Varanasi and taught for many years, travelling across north India. He passed away at **Kushinagar**.

**Core teachings**

- **Four Noble Truths**: life involves suffering (*dukkha*); suffering arises from craving; suffering can end; the way to end it is the Eightfold Path.
- **The Eightfold Path**: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration.
- **The Middle Path**: avoid both extreme luxury and extreme self-punishment.
- **Ahimsa** (non-violence) and **compassion** (*karuna*) for all beings.
- Everything changes — nothing is permanent.

He taught in **Pali/Prakrit**, the language of ordinary people, so everyone could understand. His followers formed the **sangha** (community of monks and nuns). Buddhism later spread across Asia — to Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, China, Korea, Japan, Tibet — especially after Emperor Ashoka supported it.

Dukkha — suffering
Middle Path — avoiding extremes

check.q: Where did the Buddha give his first sermon?
check.why: After enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, the Buddha gave his first teaching at Sarnath near Varanasi.

sections.md:
Jain tradition holds that its teachings were taught by a line of **24 Tirthankaras** ('ford-makers' who help people cross the river of rebirth). The 23rd was **Parshvanatha**, and the 24th was **Vardhamana Mahavira**, who lived around the same period as the Buddha.

Mahavira was born into a royal family near **Vaishali** (Bihar). At about 30, he left home, lived as an ascetic for about 12 years and attained **kevala jnana** (complete knowledge). He was called **Jina** ('conqueror' of the self) — and his followers are **Jains**.

**Key teachings**

- **Ahimsa** — total non-violence towards all living beings, even tiny insects. Some Jain monks sweep the path softly and cover their mouths to avoid harming creatures.
- **Satya** (truth), **asteya** (not stealing), **brahmacharya** (self-control), **aparigraha** (non-possession — not being attached to things).
- **Anekantavada** — the idea that reality has many sides and no single viewpoint holds the whole truth. The classic illustration is the story of blind men touching an elephant: one feels the trunk and says 'a snake', another the leg and says 'a pillar'. Each is partly right. This idea encourages listening to others' views.

Jain communities contributed greatly to Indian literature, mathematics, trade and art — like the Dilwara temples at Mount Abu and the huge statue of Bahubali (Gommateshwara) at Shravanabelagola, Karnataka.

check.q: The Jain idea that truth has many sides and no single view sees all of it is called:
check.why: Anekantavada, illustrated by the blind men and the elephant, teaches the many-sidedness of reality.

sections.md:
Not all roots are found in books. Alongside these texts, India's **folk** and **tribal** communities developed rich traditions passed down orally and through practice — songs, dances, stories, crafts and knowledge of forests, rivers and medicinal plants.

Some common features:

- **Nature is sacred.** Many communities worship hills, rivers, trees, animals and the Earth. Sacred groves — *devrai* in Maharashtra, *kavu* in Kerala, *orans* in Rajasthan, *sarna* among some communities in Jharkhand — are protected forest patches where no tree is cut.
- **Community and sharing.** Harvests and festivals are celebrated together.
- **Deep knowledge** of local ecology — which plant heals, when the rains come.

Examples: the **Bishnoi** community of Rajasthan is famous for protecting trees and blackbucks; the Warli painting tradition of Maharashtra; festivals like Sarhul in Jharkhand; Pithora painting among the Rathwa of Gujarat.

These traditions and the textual traditions influenced each other. Many deities, festivals and ideas moved between villages and scriptures. That two-way flow is why Indian culture became like the banyan — **many roots, one tree**.

check.q: What is a sacred grove?
options: A patch of forest protected by a community for religious reasons
check.why: Sacred groves are community-protected forests where cutting trees is forbidden, helping preserve biodiversity.

sections.h: Shared values: the trunk of the banyan
sections.md:
Look across all these roots and you find ideas that keep returning, even though the traditions differ in many ways:

| Value | Where we meet it |
|---|---|
| **Dharma** — right conduct, duty | From Vedic *rita* to Buddhist and Jain teaching |
| **Ahimsa** — non-violence | Upanishads, Buddha, Mahavira; later Gandhi |
| **Karma** — actions have results | Upanishads, Buddhism, Jainism |
| **Respect for nature** | Vedic hymns, sacred groves, Bishnoi practice |
| **Questioning and debate** | Nasadiya Sukta, Upanishadic dialogues, darshanas |
| **Accepting many views** | 'Truth is one, called by many names'; anekantavada |
| **Seva and sharing** | Community feasts, care for guests and the needy |

These shared values helped very different communities live side by side and learn from one another. They also travelled far: Buddhism shaped cultures across Asia; yoga and meditation are practised worldwide; **Mahatma Gandhi** drew on ahimsa for India's freedom struggle; and the **Chipko** movement in the Himalayas, where villagers hugged trees to save them, echoed the Bishnoi spirit.

> Think about it: Which of these values do you see in your own family, school or neighbourhood? Which would you most like to practise more?

check.q: Which value appears in the Upanishads, Buddhism and Jainism and later inspired Gandhi?
check.why: Ahimsa, non-violence, is central to all three traditions and became the heart of Gandhi's struggle.

story.title: Nachiketa at the Door of Death (a retelling from the Katha Upanishad)

parts.md:
Long ago, a man named Vajashravas held a great ritual and gave away gifts — but only his old, useless cows. His young son **Nachiketa** felt this was not true giving. "Father, to whom will you give me?" he asked. He asked again, and again. Annoyed, his father snapped, "To Death I give you!"

Nachiketa took the words seriously. He went to the house of **Yama**, the lord of death. Yama was away, and the boy waited at the door for three days and nights without food or water.

When Yama returned, he was ashamed that a guest had waited so long. "Choose three boons," he said. Nachiketa asked first that his father be calm and welcome him home; second, to learn a sacred fire ritual. Both were granted at once.

For the third, Nachiketa asked: "What happens to a person after death? Tell me the truth of the self." Yama hesitated. "Ask for anything else — long life, cattle, gold, kingdoms, music and dancing!" But Nachiketa replied that all such things fade. "Keep your riches. I want to know the truth."

Pleased by the boy's steadiness, Yama taught him that the true self, the Atman, is not born and does not die; it is not destroyed when the body is destroyed. He explained that wise people choose the *good* (shreyas) over the merely *pleasant* (preyas).

Nachiketa returned home with knowledge greater than any treasure. The story is still told to show that a sincere question, asked with courage, is worth more than riches.

summary: Indian culture is like a banyan tree — many roots and branches forming one whole.
There are four Vedas: Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva; the Rig Veda is the oldest.
The Vedas were preserved orally with great precision; Vedic chanting is UNESCO-recognised heritage.
Vedic ideas include rita (cosmic order), respect for nature, open questioning and assemblies (sabha, samiti).
The Upanishads explore Brahman (ultimate reality) and Atman (self), teaching their oneness; Gargi and Maitreyi took part in debates.
Six classical darshanas: Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta; Charvaka was a sceptical school.
Patanjali's Yoga Sutras; 21 June is International Day of Yoga.
The Buddha: born Lumbini, enlightened at Bodh Gaya, first sermon at Sarnath, died at Kushinagar.
Buddhism teaches the Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path and Middle Path; it spread across Asia.
Mahavira was the 24th Tirthankara; Jainism stresses ahimsa, five vows and anekantavada.
Folk and tribal traditions treat nature as sacred and protect sacred groves.
Shared values — dharma, ahimsa, karma, respect for nature, debate, many views, seva — link all the roots.

glossary.d: A system of philosophy; 'way of seeing'.
In Jainism, a teacher who shows the way across the cycle of rebirth.
Non-violence.
Buddhist monastic community.
Philosophical texts; literally 'sitting near' a teacher.

rd-school-c6-social-b.ch08-unity-diversi.title: Unity in Diversity, or 'Many in the One'
rd-school-c6-social-b.ch08-unity-diversi.subtitle: Rice and roti, saris and stories, a hundred festivals — and the threads that tie them into one fabric

sections.md:
Board the **Vivek Express**, one of India's longest train routes, at Dibrugarh in Assam and get off at Kanniyakumari, about 4,200 km and roughly three days later. On the way, your food changes: fish curry and rice in Assam, *machher jhol* in Bengal, *dalma* in Odisha, spicy *pulihora* in Andhra, and finally *sambar*, *rasam* and coconut chutney in Tamil Nadu. Announcements at stations switch from Assamese to Bengali, Odia, Telugu, Tamil. Clothes, scripts on signboards and temple shapes change too.

Yet everyone on the train calls themselves Indian. Fellow passengers share snacks, children play together, and the same cricket score excites the whole coach.

This is what we mean by **unity in diversity** — or as the chapter title puts it, **'many in the one'**. India's diversity is like the many colours of a rainbow, which together make one arc of light.

In this chapter we explore:

- the **diversity** of India's land, languages, food, clothing and festivals;
- the **unity** that runs beneath — shared values, stories, ideas, arts and history;
- how diversity and unity are not opposites but **strengthen each other**.

India is vast — over 32 lakh square kilometres — with snowy mountains, deserts, plains, plateaus, forests, coasts and islands. Different landscapes and climates have led people to develop different ways of living: stone houses with sloping roofs in Himachal, bamboo homes on stilts in Assam, thick-walled mud houses in Rajasthan, airy tiled houses in Kerala.

India also has many **communities**: people of different regions, languages, religions and tribes. Our Constitution recognises 22 languages in its **Eighth Schedule**, and censuses have recorded well over a thousand mother tongues. Followers of Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism, Zoroastrianism (Parsis), Judaism and tribal faiths live together.

This diversity is not new. For thousands of years, people moved within the subcontinent and others came from outside — traders, travellers, refugees, scholars. Ideas, crafts and words travelled with them and blended into Indian life.

check.q: How many languages are listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution?
check.why: The Eighth Schedule currently lists 22 scheduled languages.

sections.h: Unity in language: words and scripts that travel
sections.md:
With so many languages, how do Indians understand each other? There are deeper links than you might think.

- **Shared word-stock.** Words travel freely between Indian languages. *Kamal* (lotus), *nagar* (town), *jal* (water) appear in many northern and southern languages; Tamil words like *kattumaram* gave English 'catamaran', and Malayalam *inchi* is linked to 'ginger'. Persian and Arabic gave Hindi, Urdu, Marathi, Bengali and others words like *kitab*, *darwaza*, *zameen*.
- **Related scripts.** Most Indian scripts — Devanagari, Bengali, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Odia, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, and even Sinhala, Thai and Tibetan — descend from the ancient **Brahmi** script of Ashoka's time. That is why their alphabets follow the same order: vowels first, then consonants grouped by where in the mouth they are spoken (*ka, kha, ga…*).
- **Bilingual living.** Most Indians speak two or three languages — a Kannada-speaking child in Bengaluru may use Hindi with a friend, English in class and Tamil with a neighbour.

So India's languages are less like separate islands and more like a family of rivers that keep meeting.

check.q: Most Indian scripts descend from which ancient script?
check.why: Brahmi, used in Ashoka's inscriptions, is the ancestor of most scripts of South and Southeast Asia.

sections.md:
Indian food varies wildly — but look closer and you find shared patterns:

- **Staple + accompaniment.** Almost everywhere, a meal has a staple (rice, wheat roti, millet bhakri, ragi mudde) with dal or a vegetable or fish curry.
- **Spices** like turmeric, cumin, coriander, ginger and black pepper are used across regions, though in different combinations. Black pepper from Kerala was once so precious it was called 'black gold' in world trade.
- **The thali** — a plate with small bowls of many dishes — exists in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Odisha, Tamil Nadu and beyond. In the south, the same idea is served on a banana leaf.
- **Ideas about food**: food is often seen as sacred (*prasad*), meant to be shared (langar in gurudwaras feeds anyone who comes), and balanced for health — many traditions speak of six tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent and astringent.
- **Millets** — jowar, bajra, ragi — were eaten across India for millennia. The United Nations declared **2023 the International Year of Millets**, an idea proposed by India.

So the dishes differ, but the *grammar* of the meal is shared.

check.q: Which idea about food is shared across many Indian regions?
options: A staple served with several accompaniments
check.why: Whether rice, roti or ragi, most Indian meals pair a staple with dal, vegetables or curry — the thali pattern.

sections.h: Unity in clothing: the story of the sari
sections.md:
Clothing in India changes with climate and community: woollen *pherans* in Kashmir, *mekhela chador* in Assam, *mundu* and *veshti* in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, *ghagra-choli* in Rajasthan, *kurta-pyjama*, *salwar-kameez*, the *dhoti*, the turban tied in dozens of regional styles.

The **sari** is a wonderful example of many-in-one. It is basically an **unstitched length of cloth**, usually 5 to 9 yards (about 4.5 to 8 m), worn across much of India. Yet:

- it is **draped in over a hundred ways** — the Nivi style, the Bengali style with pleats and a key-bunch on the pallu, the Maharashtrian *nauvari* tucked like a dhoti, the Coorgi style with pleats at the back, the Gujarati style with the pallu in front;
- it is **woven differently** in each region: Banarasi silk (Uttar Pradesh), Kanjeevaram (Tamil Nadu), Paithani (Maharashtra), Patola (Gujarat), Baluchari (West Bengal), Sambalpuri and Bomkai (Odisha), Muga silk (Assam), Pochampally ikat (Telangana), Chanderi (Madhya Pradesh).

Ancient sculptures and texts show draped unstitched garments going back thousands of years. India's **handloom** heritage is so important that **7 August** is observed as **National Handloom Day**, recalling the Swadeshi movement launched on 7 August 1905.

head: Sari style
Region
fig.caption: One garment, many weaves.

check.q: Why is the sari a good example of 'many in the one'?
options: It is worn only in one state
It is one basic garment draped and woven in many regional ways
It is always made of the same cloth
check.why: The sari is a single unstitched garment found across India, yet each region has its own weave and drape.

sections.md:
India celebrates hundreds of festivals. Many share **themes** even when names differ:

**Harvest festivals** mark the gathering of crops, usually in mid-January when the Sun enters Makara (Capricorn), and again in spring or autumn:

| Festival | Region |
|---|---|
| Makar Sankranti | Many states |
| Pongal | Tamil Nadu |
| Lohri | Punjab |
| Magh Bihu / Bhogali Bihu | Assam |
| Uttarayan (kite festival) | Gujarat |
| Onam | Kerala (harvest in Aug–Sept) |
| Baisakhi | Punjab (spring harvest) |
| Nuakhai | Odisha |

**New Year festivals** in spring: Ugadi (Karnataka, Andhra, Telangana), Gudi Padwa (Maharashtra), Puthandu (Tamil Nadu), Vishu (Kerala), Bohag Bihu (Assam), Pohela Boishakh (Bengal), Baisakhi (Punjab), Navreh (Kashmir) — all around March–April.

**Festivals of light** — Diwali, Kartik Purnima, Dev Deepawali; and festivals like Christmas and Guru Nanak Jayanti are celebrated with lights too.

Indians also share in each other's festivals: neighbours exchange sweets at Eid, Diwali and Christmas; everyone flies kites at Uttarayan; people of all communities visit Durga Puja pandals.

The common threads: gratitude to nature, the turning of seasons, sharing food, family gatherings and new beginnings.

fig.caption: Different festivals, shared joy.

check.q: Pongal, Lohri, Bihu and Makar Sankranti share which common theme?
check.why: All are celebrated around mid-January to thank nature for the harvest as the Sun moves northward.

sections.h: Unity in music, dance and art
sections.md:
India's arts also show many forms built on shared foundations.

- **Music.** Hindustani music in the north and Carnatic music in the south sound different, yet both rest on the same ideas of **raga** (melodic framework) and **tala** (rhythmic cycle), with roots traced to old texts like the *Natyashastra*. Folk songs — Baul songs of Bengal, Lavani of Maharashtra, Bihu songs of Assam — sing of love, harvest and the divine in local tongues.
- **Dance.** Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (north India), Kathakali and Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur) and Sattriya (Assam) are recognised classical dances. Each has its own costume and style, but all use **mudras** (hand gestures) and **abhinaya** (expression) to tell stories, often from the epics.
- **Art and craft.** Madhubani (Bihar), Warli (Maharashtra), Pattachitra (Odisha), Gond (Madhya Pradesh), Kalamkari (Andhra Pradesh) — different styles, shared love of nature, gods and village life. **Rangoli**, *kolam*, *alpana* and *mandana* are floor designs made at doorsteps across India under different names.

> Did you know? The *kolam* drawn with rice flour at Tamil doorsteps each morning also feeds ants and birds — an artwork that is also an act of sharing.

check.q: What do Bharatanatyam, Kathak and Odissi have in common?
options: They are all from one state
They use mudras and expressions to tell stories
check.why: All classical dances share a common grammar of hand gestures and expression, though each has its own style.

sections.h: Unity in stories, ideas and history
sections.md:
**Shared stories.** The **Ramayana** and **Mahabharata** are told in nearly every Indian language and art form, each with local flavour: Kamban's Tamil Ramayana, Krittivas's Bengali Ramayana, Tulsidas's *Ramcharitmanas* in Awadhi, Ezhuthachan's Malayalam version, and many folk, tribal and Southeast Asian versions — Ramlila, Kathakali, Yakshagana, shadow puppetry. The **Panchatantra** fables travelled from India to Persia, Arabia and Europe over centuries.

**Shared sacred geography.** Pilgrims have long criss-crossed the land: to the four *dhams* (Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri, Rameswaram), the *jyotirlingas*, the *shakti peethas*, Buddhist sites like Bodh Gaya, Sikh gurudwaras like Hemkund Sahib and the Golden Temple, Sufi shrines like Ajmer Sharif, churches like Bom Jesus in Goa. A pilgrim from Kerala at a shrine in the Himalayas experiences the land as one.

**Shared values.** Respect for elders, hospitality (*atithi devo bhava*, 'the guest is like a god'), care for nature, non-violence, and the idea of the world as one family — *vasudhaiva kutumbakam* (a phrase from the Maha Upanishad) — are widely shared.

**Shared history and Constitution.** People from every region fought together in the freedom struggle. Our **Constitution** protects everyone's right to their language, religion and culture while making all citizens equal. The national anthem names regions from Punjab to Banga and from the Vindhyas and Himalayas to the seas.

> Did you know? The Indian rupee note carries its value in 15 languages on its language panel, besides Hindi and English on the front.

check.q: Vasudhaiva kutumbakam means:
check.why: The phrase from the Maha Upanishad means the whole world is one family.

sections.md:
Some people imagine that unity means everyone should be the same. India shows another way: **unity does not require uniformity**.

- Diversity brings **creativity** — music, food, crafts and ideas enrich one another (think of how Hindustani and Carnatic music, or Mughlai and regional cuisines, developed).
- It teaches **tolerance and respect** — learning to live with differences.
- It gives **resilience** — many ways of solving problems (dozens of water-harvesting traditions, many farming systems).

Of course, diversity can also bring misunderstanding or conflict when people stereotype each other. That is why learning about each other matters. Next time you meet a classmate from another state, ask about their festival, their food, their language — and share yours.

**Many in the one, and the one in the many** — that is the Indian way.

check.q: Which statement best captures 'unity in diversity'?
options: People with different cultures share common bonds and values
check.why: Unity in diversity means people keep their own cultures while sharing common bonds, values and identity.

parts.md: On the first day at a new school in Pune, Class 6B had students from seven states. The class teacher, Mrs Fernandes, announced a 'tiffin exchange' every Friday. Anirban brought luchi and aloo; Lalremsiami from Mizoram brought sticky rice with a little bamboo-shoot chutney; Harpreet brought aloo paratha; Meenakshi brought lemon rice; Zoya brought sheer khurma left over from Eid; Rohan brought poha with peanuts.

By December the class had a list on the wall: 'Our 32 Festivals'. They had flown kites for Sankranti with Rohan's family, eaten plum cake with Mrs Fernandes at Christmas, and learnt to say 'thank you' in nine languages.

At the annual day, 6B performed a song in which each child sang one line in their mother tongue and everyone sang the chorus together in Hindi and English. The audience could not understand every line — but they understood the whole song.

summary: India is diverse in land, climate, languages, religions, food, clothing and festivals.
The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages; India has hundreds of mother tongues.
Words travel between languages, and most Indian scripts descend from Brahmi.
Food differs but shares patterns: staple plus dishes, common spices, the thali, food as sacred and shared.
2023 was the International Year of Millets.
The sari is one unstitched garment with many regional weaves and drapes.
National Handloom Day is 7 August, recalling the Swadeshi movement of 1905.
Harvest festivals (Pongal, Lohri, Bihu, Sankranti, Onam) and spring New Years show shared themes.
Classical music rests on raga and tala; classical dances share mudras and abhinaya; folk arts share themes.
The Ramayana, Mahabharata and Panchatantra are retold across languages and art forms.
Pilgrimage routes connect all corners of India into a shared sacred geography.
Shared values: hospitality, respect for nature, non-violence, vasudhaiva kutumbakam.
The Constitution protects cultural rights and equal citizenship.
Unity does not mean uniformity; diversity is a source of strength and creativity.

glossary.d: Variety and difference.
Everything being the same.
Cloth woven by hand on a loom.
Melodic framework in Indian music.
The world is one family.

rd-school-c6-social-b.ch09-family-commun.title: Family and Community
rd-school-c6-social-b.ch09-family-commun.subtitle: The circles of care that hold us — from the kitchen to the neighbourhood and beyond

sections.h: Who caught you when you fell?

sections.md:
A **family** is a group of people related by birth, marriage or adoption who usually live together and care for one another. Families are the first place where a child learns to speak, eat, share, love and behave.

**Types of families**

- **Joint (or extended) family** — several generations live together: grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and cousins, often sharing a kitchen and resources. Traditionally common in India, especially in villages.
- **Nuclear family** — parents and their children living together. More common in cities today, as people move for jobs and education.
- Other forms — a single parent with children; children living with grandparents; families joined by adoption; relatives who live apart but stay very close.

There is no single 'correct' family. What makes a family is **care, responsibility and belonging**.

| Joint family | Nuclear family |
|---|---|
| Many generations together | Usually two generations |
| Work and costs shared by many | Fewer people share tasks |
| Children learn from grandparents | More privacy and independence |
| Elders cared for at home | Elders may live separately |

Many Indian families today are a mix: nuclear households that stay closely linked with grandparents and relatives through visits, phone calls and festivals.

Nuclear family — parents and children

check.q: Which is a feature of a joint family?
options: Only parents and children live together
Several generations share a home and responsibilities
No elders live with the family
check.why: In a joint family, grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and cousins typically live together and share tasks.

sections.md:
A **family tree** is a chart that shows how members of a family are related across generations. It looks like an upside-down tree: the oldest generation at the top, branches spreading down to children and grandchildren.

**How to make one**

1. Write your own name at the bottom centre.
2. Above you, write your parents' names, joined by a line.
3. Above each parent, write *their* parents — your four grandparents.
4. Add your parents' brothers and sisters beside them, and their children (your cousins) on your level.
5. Ask elders for names, birthplaces and occupations. Add little drawings or photographs.

While making it, you become a historian of your own family! You may discover that a great-grandfather was a weaver in Varanasi, that your family moved from a village to a city two generations ago, or that you have relatives in another state or country.

> Did you know? Many Indian languages have separate words for every relative: in Hindi, *chacha* (father's younger brother), *tau* (father's elder brother), *mama* (mother's brother), *mausi* (mother's sister), *bua* (father's sister). In Tamil, *chithappa* and *periyappa* tell younger and elder paternal uncles apart. English mostly just says 'uncle' and 'aunt'! This shows how important extended family relationships are in India.

fig.alt: Boxes for grandparents, then father and mother, then me, appearing one by one and linked by lines.

check.q: In a family tree, the oldest generation is usually shown:
check.why: Family trees put the eldest generation at the top and branch downward to younger generations.

sections.h: Roles and values learnt in the family
sections.md:
In a family, everyone has **roles** — things they do for others. Elders may earn, cook, look after the house, guide the young. Children help with small chores, study and care for younger siblings or grandparents. Roles change as we grow; a child who is cared for today will care for aging parents tomorrow.

It is important that roles are shared **fairly**. Household work — cooking, cleaning, fetching water, caring for the sick — is real and valuable work, even though it is unpaid. Boys and girls, men and women can share it equally.

Families pass on **values**:

- **Respect for elders** — greeting them first, listening to their experience.
- **Sharing and sacrifice** — the last piece of mithai goes to the youngest; parents save for children's education.
- **Responsibility and honesty**.
- **Care for the vulnerable** — the sick, the very young, the old.

Families also pass on **culture**: language, recipes, songs, stories, festival customs and skills like weaving, pottery, farming or music. A grandmother teaching a granddaughter to draw a kolam or rangoli is keeping a tradition alive.

Indian stories have long reflected family values — the Ramayana's picture of brothers' loyalty, or the Panchatantra, which was said to have been told to teach young princes wisdom. Every family also has its own stories, told and retold at mealtimes.

check.q: Why should household work be shared by everyone in the family?
options: It is valuable work and sharing it is fair
Elders must do all of it
check.why: Household work takes real time and effort, so sharing it fairly among all members is just.

check.q: Which of these is a community of interest?
check.why: A cricket club brings together people who share an interest, which is what a community of interest is.

sections.md:
Families and communities are connected like the threads of a woven cloth.

**Example 1: A village wedding.** Relatives cook, neighbours lend utensils and cots, friends decorate, musicians play. Costs and work are shared, so no single family carries the whole burden.

**Example 2: Water.** In many dry villages of Rajasthan and Gujarat, communities have for centuries built and cared for *johads*, *kunds* and *talabs*. Each family contributes labour to desilt the pond before the monsoon. Everyone benefits.

**Example 3: Care for elders.** When a family member works in another city, neighbours often check on elderly parents. Many communities run daycare centres for seniors.

**Example 4: Traditional knowledge.** Knowledge of seeds, medicinal plants, weather signs and crafts is held by communities and passed through families.

**Example 5: Disasters.** When cyclones strike Odisha's coast, village volunteers, fishermen with boats and local youth help move families to cyclone shelters — a big reason why loss of life has fallen sharply in recent cyclones.

**Community helpers** — sweepers, postmen, vegetable sellers, the *anganwadi* worker, the ASHA health worker, the school bus driver — are part of our community. We depend on them, and they deserve respect and thanks.

fig.caption: Community work: families together restore a village pond before the monsoon.
fig.alt: Villagers working beside a pond that grows larger, with houses in the background.

check.q: A gurudwara langar is an example of:
options: A community kitchen that serves free food to all
check.why: Langar is a community kitchen run by volunteers that feeds anyone without charge.

sections.md:
Families and communities are meant to protect their members. Most do, every day. But sometimes people need extra support — and society, through laws and public services, steps in to help.

- **Children** have the right to education (free and compulsory schooling from 6 to 14 years under the Right to Education Act, 2009), to health, to play and to safety. Child helpline **1098** is a free number anyone can call if a child needs help.
- **Elders** deserve care and dignity. India has a law (2007) that makes children responsible for the maintenance of their elderly parents, and many states run old-age homes and pensions.
- **Persons with disabilities** have the right to equal opportunities and access, and communities can make spaces friendlier with ramps, sign language and patience.
- **Every member's voice matters.** Healthy families discuss decisions together and listen to children too.

Communities also have responsibilities: keeping shared spaces clean, welcoming newcomers, and making sure no one — a widow, a migrant worker, a lonely elder — is left out.

> Think about it: Is there someone in your colony or village who lives alone? What small thing could your family do for them this week?

check.q: The free helpline anyone can call when a child needs help is:
check.why: 1098 is India's Childline number, a free emergency service for children in need of care and protection.

sections.md:
Families and communities are changing:

- More people move to cities for work — so more **nuclear families** and **migrants**.
- Many elders live alone while children work far away.
- Smaller families, more children going to school and college, more women working outside the home.
- Phones and video calls help families stay close across distances.

These changes bring both opportunities and challenges. New kinds of community grow — resident welfare associations, self-help groups of women, online groups of parents, senior citizens' clubs.

What stays important is the spirit of **mutual care**. The ancient phrase ***vasudhaiva kutumbakam*** — 'the world is one family' — reminds us that our circle of care can extend to all humanity and even to all living beings. India chose a theme based on it for its G20 presidency in 2023 (*One Earth, One Family, One Future*).

check.q: Which change has led to more nuclear families in India?
options: People moving to cities for work and education
check.why: Migration to cities for jobs and studies often leads parents and children to set up separate, smaller households.

parts.md:
When Meera's grandmother came to live with them in their two-room flat in Pune, Meera was not pleased. She had to share her room. Dadi woke at five, chanted softly, and asked too many questions about homework.

One rainy evening the power failed. Mummy was late from work, Papa was stuck in traffic. Dadi lit a lamp, opened an old notebook with yellow pages, and said, "Come, let us make *thalipeeth*." In the notebook were recipes in four handwritings — Dadi's, her mother's, an aunt's, and one in shaky English by a neighbour from Kerala who had lived next door forty years ago.

As they cooked, Dadi told stories: how the whole chawl had shared one tap, how neighbours took turns minding each other's babies, how the Kerala neighbour had taught her appam and she had taught him puran poli.

When Mummy and Papa reached home, wet and tired, a hot meal was waiting — and Meera had flour on her nose. Next week Meera brought the recipe book to school for a project called *My Family, My Community*. She added a new page herself: her friend Zoya's mother's sheer khurma recipe. "Now it has five handwritings," said Dadi, smiling.

summary: We live within circles of care: family, neighbourhood, wider community.
A family is people related by birth, marriage or adoption who care for each other.
Types: joint/extended families, nuclear families and other forms; care makes a family.
A family tree maps relationships across generations, oldest at the top.
Indian languages have many specific kinship words, showing the importance of relatives.
Family members have roles; household work is valuable and should be shared fairly.
Families pass on values (respect, sharing, responsibility) and culture (language, recipes, crafts).
A community is a group linked by place, work, language, belief or interest that supports its members.
Communities share celebrations, resources (ponds, langars) and help in crises like cyclones.
Community helpers like ASHA and anganwadi workers deserve respect.
Laws and services protect children (RTE, helpline 1098), elders and persons with disabilities.
Families are changing with migration and urbanisation; new communities are forming.
Vasudhaiva kutumbakam: the world is one family.

glossary.d: Group of people with something in common who support each other.
Chart showing family relationships across generations.
Free community kitchen at a gurudwara.
Accredited Social Health Activist, a village health worker.
Moving from one place to another to live or work.

rd-school-c7-english.grammar-class7.title: Grammar for Class 7 — The Complete Companion
rd-school-c7-english.grammar-class7.subtitle: Parts of speech, articles, tenses, voice, reported speech, modals, clauses, word-building and punctuation — explained with Indian examples.

sections.md:
A sentence is like a train: words are the coaches, and grammar is the coupling that keeps them in order. Mix the order — *Mumbai to train the went* — and nothing moves. Grammar is not a list of punishments; it is the set of patterns that makes meaning travel safely from your mind to someone else's.

This read covers the Class 7 grammar you meet across your English book: **parts of speech, nouns, pronouns, articles and determiners, adjectives, adverbs, verbs and verb forms, tenses, subject–verb agreement, active/passive voice, direct/indirect speech, modals, question tags, prepositions, conjunctions, clauses, word-building and punctuation**.

**The eight parts of speech**

| Part | Job | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Noun | names | Riya, Kolkata, happiness |
| Pronoun | replaces a noun | she, it, they |
| Verb | action/state | run, is, seems |
| Adjective | describes noun | tall, three, Indian |
| Adverb | describes verb/adjective | quickly, very |
| Preposition | shows relation | in, on, under |
| Conjunction | joins | and, but, because |
| Interjection | emotion | Wow! Oh! |

A word's part of speech depends on **its job in that sentence**: *I like the **light*** (noun); *a **light** bag* (adjective); *please **light** the lamp* (verb).

check.q: In 'She ran quickly to the station', what part of speech is 'quickly'?
check.why: 'Quickly' tells us how she ran, so it modifies the verb and is an adverb.

sections.md:
**Nouns**
- *Common* (city), *proper* (Jaipur), *collective* (a team, a flock), *abstract* (honesty), *material* (gold).
- **Countable** (two mangoes) vs **uncountable** (rice, water, information). Say *much rice*, *many mangoes*; *less sugar*, *fewer chairs*.
- Gender and number: *tiger–tigress, actor–actress*; plurals *child–children, mouse–mice, leaf–leaves, sheep–sheep*.

**Pronouns**
- Personal: I, you, he, she, it, we, they (subject) / me, him, her, us, them (object). *Between you and **me*** (not *I*).
- Reflexive: myself, themselves — *Ravi hurt himself.*
- Relative: who, whom, whose, which, that.
- Possessive: mine, yours, hers.

**Adjectives and degrees of comparison**

| Positive | Comparative | Superlative |
|---|---|---|
| tall | taller | tallest |
| happy | happier | happiest |
| beautiful | more beautiful | most beautiful |
| good | better | best |
| bad | worse | worst |
| little | less | least |

*Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world. K2 is higher than Kangchenjunga.* Never double up: not *more taller*.

**Order of adjectives** (opinion-size-age-shape-colour-origin-material-purpose): *a lovely small old round red Kashmiri woollen shawl* — long, but correct!

**Adverbs** tell how (*slowly*), when (*yesterday*), where (*here*), how often (*always, never*) and how much (*very, too*). Frequency adverbs usually go before the main verb: *She **always** walks to school.*

check.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: There is less chairs in the hall.
There are fewer chairs in the hall.
There are less chair in the hall.
There is fewer chairs in the hall.
check.why: Chairs are countable, so we use 'fewer' and the plural verb 'are'.

sections.md:
**Determiners** are little words that come before a noun to show *which* or *how many*: articles (a, an, the), demonstratives (this, that, these, those), quantifiers (some, any, many, much, few, little, each, every), possessives (my, your, their) and numbers.

**A or an?** It depends on the **sound**, not the letter:
- *a* before a consonant sound: *a book, a university* (you-), *a one-rupee coin* (wun-).
- *an* before a vowel sound: *an apple, an hour* (silent h), *an MLA* (em-), *an honest man*.

**When to use 'the'**
- Something already mentioned or known: *I saw a dog. **The** dog was barking.*
- Unique things: *the sun, the moon, the sky*.
- Rivers, seas, oceans, mountain ranges, groups of islands: *the Ganga, the Arabian Sea, the Himalayas, the Andamans*.
- Superlatives and ordinals: *the best, the first*.
- Famous books and newspapers: *the Ramayana, the Hindu*.

**No article** before names of people, cities, single mountains, languages, meals and games: *Mount Everest, Hindi, lunch, cricket* — *We play cricket after lunch.*

**Few vs a few; little vs a little**: *a few friends* (some — positive), *few friends* (hardly any — negative). *A little milk* (some), *little milk* (almost none).

check.q: Fill in: 'He is ___ honest boy and wants to join ___ Indian Army.'
check.why: 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound (silent h), and 'the Indian Army' is a specific, unique institution.

sections.md:
**Transitive and intransitive.** A *transitive* verb needs an object: *Meena **reads** a book.* An *intransitive* verb does not: *The baby **sleeps**.* Some verbs are both: *He **sang** (a song).* Only transitive verbs can be made passive.

**Main and helping verbs.** In *She **is** writing*, *is* helps the main verb *writing*. Helping (auxiliary) verbs: *be (am, is, are, was, were), have, do*, and the modals.

**The three forms**: base (V1) *go*, past (V2) *went*, past participle (V3) *gone*. Regular verbs add *-ed* (*play–played–played*); irregular verbs must be learnt: *write–wrote–written, eat–ate–eaten, begin–began–begun, bring–brought–brought, cut–cut–cut*.

**Non-finite forms** — verb forms that do not show tense:
- **Infinitive** (to + V1): *I want **to learn** the sitar.*
- **Gerund** (V-ing used as a noun): ***Swimming** is good exercise. She enjoys **dancing**.*
- **Participle** (V-ing or V3 used as an adjective): *a **running** tap, a **broken** pot*.

Some verbs take a gerund (*enjoy, avoid, finish, mind*), others an infinitive (*want, decide, hope, agree*): *She finished **writing**; she decided **to write**.*

check.q: In 'Reading at night strains the eyes', the word 'Reading' is a:
check.why: 'Reading' is a verb-ing form acting as the subject noun of the sentence, which makes it a gerund.

sections.md:
English has three times (past, present, future) and four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous) — twelve tenses. Using the verb *play*:

| | Simple | Continuous | Perfect | Perfect continuous |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Present | plays | is playing | has played | has been playing |
| Past | played | was playing | had played | had been playing |
| Future | will play | will be playing | will have played | will have been playing |

**When to use**
- Simple present: habits and facts — *The sun rises in the east.*
- Present continuous: now — *It is raining.*
- Present perfect: past action linked to now — *I have finished my homework.* (no specific past time; don't say *I have finished yesterday*).
- Past continuous for a longer action interrupted by a shorter one: *I **was bathing** when the phone **rang**.*
- Past perfect: the earlier of two past actions — *The train **had left** before we **reached** the station.*
- Perfect continuous: duration — *She has been practising the violin since 6 o'clock / for two hours.*

**since vs for**: *since* + point of time (since Monday, since 2020); *for* + period (for three days).

check.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have seen that film yesterday.
I had see that film yesterday.
I am seeing that film yesterday.
check.why: With a specific past time like 'yesterday', English uses the simple past, not the present perfect.

sections.md:
The verb must agree with its subject in number.

- *The boy **plays**. The boys **play**.*
- Words between subject and verb don't change it: *The box of mangoes **is** heavy.* (subject = box)
- *Each, every, everyone, nobody, either, neither* take singular: *Everyone **has** arrived.*
- *Neither the teacher nor the students **were** late* — the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
- Two subjects joined by *and* take plural: *Ravi and Sita **are** here.* But *Bread and butter **is** my breakfast* (one dish).
- Collective nouns usually singular in Indian/British usage when the group acts as one: *The team **is** strong.*
- *Ten kilometres **is** a long walk* (amount as one unit).
- *The news **is** good. Mathematics **is** fun.*

check.q: Fill in: 'One of my friends ___ a cricketer.'
check.why: The subject is 'one', which is singular, so the verb is 'is'.

sections.md:
In the **active** voice the doer comes first: *Tendulkar hit the ball.* In the **passive**, the receiver comes first: *The ball was hit by Tendulkar.*

**Recipe**: object → subject; *be* in the same tense + past participle; doer after *by* (optional).

| Tense | Active | Passive |
|---|---|---|
| Simple present | She writes a letter. | A letter is written by her. |
| Present continuous | She is writing a letter. | A letter is being written. |
| Present perfect | She has written a letter. | A letter has been written. |
| Simple past | She wrote a letter. | A letter was written. |
| Future | She will write a letter. | A letter will be written. |
| Modal | You must finish it. | It must be finished. |

**Commands** become *let* sentences: *Open the door* → *Let the door be opened.*

**Use the passive** when the doer is unknown or unimportant: *The Taj Mahal was built in the 17th century. My bicycle has been stolen!* Notices and science reports use it a lot: *The solution was heated for five minutes.*

check.q: Passive of 'The workers are building a bridge':
options: A bridge is built by the workers.
A bridge was being built by the workers.
A bridge is being built by the workers.
A bridge has built the workers.
check.why: Present continuous passive uses 'is/are being' + past participle.

sections.md:
**Direct**: *Paati said, "I am tired."* **Indirect**: *Paati said that she was tired.*

**Rules when the reporting verb is past**
1. Change pronouns to fit the reporter.
2. Backshift tense: is → was; am/are → was/were; has → had; will → would; can → could; simple past → had + V3.
3. Change time/place words: now → then; today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the day before; here → there; this → that.
4. Questions: *He asked, "Where do you live?"* → *He asked where I lived.* (no question mark; normal word order). Yes/no questions use *if/whether*: *She asked if I was hungry.*
5. Commands: *"Sit down," said the teacher* → *The teacher told us to sit down.* Requests: *asked/requested … to*. Negative commands: *told us not to …*
6. Exclamations: *He said, "What a lovely garden!"* → *He exclaimed that it was a very lovely garden.*
7. Universal truths keep present tense: *He said that the earth goes round the sun.*

check.q: Indirect speech: He said, "I will come tomorrow."
options: He said that he will come tomorrow.
He said that he would come the next day.
He said that I would come tomorrow.
He says he came the next day.
check.why: 'Will' backshifts to 'would', 'I' becomes 'he', and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.

sections.h: Modals, question tags, prepositions and conjunctions
sections.md:
**Modals** add mood: *can/could* (ability), *may/might* (permission/possibility), *must* (necessity), *should* (advice), *will/would* (future/polite), *need not* (no necessity), *ought to* (duty). Modals take the base verb: *She can **swim***, not *can swims*.

**Question tags** check or confirm. Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag, using the same helping verb and a pronoun:
- *It is hot, **isn't it**?* — *You don't like karela, **do you**?* — *She can dance, **can't she**?* — *They went home, **didn't they**?* — *I am late, **aren't I**?* (special case) — *Let's go, **shall we**?*

**Prepositions of time**: *at* 6 p.m., *on* Monday / 15 August, *in* July / 2024 / the morning.
**Place**: *at* the bus stop, *on* the table, *in* the box; *between* two, *among* many.

**Conjunctions**
- Coordinating (FANBOYS): for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.
- Subordinating: because, although, if, unless, when, while, since, until.
- Correlative pairs: either…or, neither…nor, not only…but also, both…and.

*Although it was raining, the match continued.* (never *Although…but*)

check.q: Add the correct tag: 'Rohan never misses practice, ___?'
check.why: 'Never' makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive: 'does he?'

sections.md:
A **clause** has a subject and a verb. A **main clause** stands alone; a **subordinate clause** depends on it.

- *Simple*: one main clause — *The bell rang.*
- *Compound*: two main clauses joined — *The bell rang and we ran out.*
- *Complex*: main + subordinate — *When the bell rang, we ran out.*

**Relative clauses**: *The girl **who won the quiz** is my cousin. The book **which you lent me** is great.*

**Kinds of sentences by purpose**: declarative (*I like tea.*), interrogative (*Do you like tea?*), imperative (*Make some tea.*), exclamatory (*What lovely tea!*).

**Punctuation toolkit**
- Full stop, question mark, exclamation mark end sentences.
- Comma: lists (*mangoes, bananas and grapes*), after introductory phrases, around extra information.
- Apostrophe: possession (*Ravi's bat, the girls' room*) and contractions (*don't, it's = it is*). *Its* (possession) has no apostrophe!
- Quotation marks for direct speech.
- Capital letters for names, places, days, months, and *I*.

check.q: Which sentence is complex?
options: Because it was late, we took an auto.
check.why: It has a subordinate clause ('Because it was late') attached to a main clause.

sections.h: Word-building: prefixes, suffixes, phrasal verbs, and confusing pairs
sections.md:
**Prefixes** change meaning: *un*happy, *dis*agree, *im*possible, *in*correct, *mis*understand, *re*write, *pre*view.

**Suffixes** often change the part of speech: *kind → kind**ness*** (noun), *care → care**ful*** (adjective), *quick → quick**ly*** (adverb), *beauty → beauti**fy*** (verb), *teach → teach**er***.

**Synonyms and antonyms**: *brave–courageous; ancient–modern; generous–mean*.

**Phrasal verbs** (verb + small word) have special meanings:
- *look after* (take care of), *look up* (search a word), *give up* (stop trying), *put off* (postpone), *run out of* (have none left), *take after* (resemble a relative), *turn down* (refuse), *break down* (stop working).

*We ran out of milk, so the match was put off until Dadi looked after the guests* — three in one sentence!

**Homophones and confusing pairs**

| Pair | Example |
|---|---|
| their / there / they're | They're putting their bags there. |
| your / you're | You're forgetting your umbrella. |
| its / it's | It's wagging its tail. |
| lose / loose | Don't lose your loose button. |
| accept / except | All except Ravi accepted the invitation. |
| affect / effect | Noise affects sleep; it has a bad effect. |

check.q: 'Priya takes after her grandmother' means Priya:
check.why: The phrasal verb 'take after' means to look or behave like an older relative.

workedExamples.q: Change to passive: 'Who wrote this letter?'
steps: Question in simple past with 'who' as subject.
Object 'this letter' becomes subject; use 'by whom'.
Form: By whom + was + subject + past participle.
workedExamples.answer: By whom was this letter written?

workedExamples.q: Report: The teacher said to me, "Have you finished your work?"
workedExamples.answer: The teacher asked me if I had finished my work.

workedExamples.q: Correct: 'Neither of the boys have done their homework.'
workedExamples.answer: Neither of the boys has done his homework.

workedExamples.q: Combine using 'who': 'I met a man. He had climbed Everest.'
steps: Identify the shared noun: a man / he.
workedExamples.answer: I met a man who had climbed Everest.

workedExamples.q: Fill in articles: '___ elephant and ___ one-horned rhino live in ___ Kaziranga National Park.'
steps: 'elephant' starts with a vowel sound → an.
A specific named park with 'National Park' usually takes 'the'.
workedExamples.answer: An elephant and a one-horned rhino live in the Kaziranga National Park.

workedExamples.q: Add question tags: (a) You can swim. (b) She hasn't eaten.
workedExamples.answer: (a) You can swim, can't you? (b) She hasn't eaten, has she?

summary: A word's part of speech depends on its job in the sentence.
Countable nouns: many/fewer; uncountable: much/less.
'A/an' depends on the first sound; 'the' for known, unique and named rivers, seas and ranges.
Comparatives compare two; superlatives compare three or more.
Transitive verbs take objects; infinitives, gerunds and participles are non-finite forms.
Twelve tenses = 3 times × 4 aspects; don't use the present perfect with a specific past time.
since + point of time; for + period.
Verbs agree with the true subject; each/every take singular.
Passive: be + past participle, used when the doer is unimportant.
Indirect speech backshifts tense and changes pronouns and time words.
Modals take the base form; question tags reverse the polarity of the statement.
Simple, compound and complex sentences differ by clauses.
Prefixes and suffixes build new words; phrasal verbs have special meanings.
'Its' = possession; 'it's' = it is.
practice: Identify the part of speech of 'fast' in: (a) He runs fast. (b) a fast train. (c) They fast on Ekadashi.
Fill in a/an/the: ___ hour ago, I saw ___ European tourist near ___ Gateway of India.
Write the comparative and superlative of: good, busy, famous, little.
Pick out the gerund and the infinitive: 'She loves painting and wants to become an artist.'
Fill in with the correct tense: 'By the time the doctor ___ (arrive), the patient ___ (recover).'
Change into passive: 'The children will plant trees tomorrow.'
Change into indirect speech: Mother said, "Don't play in the rain."
Add question tags: 'Let's begin', 'He wasn't listening', 'I am right'.
Correct the errors: 'He don't know where is the station.'
Combine using 'although': 'He was tired. He finished the race.'
Punctuate: lets go to amits house said priya its only five minutes away
Make new words using un-, dis-, -ful and -ness, and use any four phrasal verbs in sentences.

rd-school-c7-english.revision-practice.title: Class 7 English — Whole-Book Revision
rd-school-c7-english.revision-practice.subtitle: Every Honeycomb chapter and poem, plus the supplementary reader, in one place: plots, characters, themes, devices and the questions examiners love.

sections.md:
Ten units, ten stories, nine poems, a supplementary reader — and an exam in a few weeks. This read compresses the whole book into quick-recall retellings, theme maps and practice questions. All retellings below are in our own words; read the original chapters in your free NCERT textbook.

**Study plan.** Read one section a day, then close the screen and say the key points aloud. Testing yourself beats rereading. Make a one-line 'hook' for each story (e.g., *Gessler — boots too good to need replacing*).

**Exam answer formula**: *Point → Evidence from the text → Explanation.* For a 3-mark question write 50–60 words; for a long answer, 100–120 words. Always name the character and the chapter.

head: Unit
Prose (author)
Poem (poet)
rows: Gopal and the Hilsa Fish (folk tale)
The Ashes That Made Trees Bloom (Japanese folk tale)
Mystery of the Talking Fan (Maude Rubin)

sections.h: Unit 1 — Three Questions and The Squirrel
sections.md:
**Three Questions (retold).** A king believes he would never fail if he knew three things: the right time to begin anything, the right people to listen to, and the most important thing to do. He offers a reward, but learned men give conflicting answers — keep a timetable, consult a council, ask magicians, follow doctors or soldiers. Unsatisfied, he goes in plain clothes to a hermit famous for wisdom. The frail hermit is digging; the king takes the spade and digs for hours. A bearded man runs out of the wood, bleeding from a stomach wound. The king washes and bandages him and lets him rest in the hut. Next morning the man confesses: he was the king's enemy, had come to kill him in revenge for a brother's death and the seizure of his property, but was wounded by the king's bodyguards. Now he asks forgiveness and promises loyalty. The king forgives him and promises to return his property.

The hermit then explains that the questions are already answered: had the king not pitied him and stayed to dig, the man would have attacked him on the way back. So the most important **time** is **now**, the only time we have power over; the most important **person** is the one we are with; and the most important **thing** is to do that person good.

**Themes:** wisdom, kindness, forgiveness, living in the present. **Exam favourites:** Why did the king go to the hermit in simple clothes? (The hermit received only simple folk, and the king wanted honest advice.) Why did the enemy become a friend? (The king saved his life.)

**The Squirrel (meaning).** The poet watches a small grey squirrel with a tail curved like a question mark. It circles round a tree trunk to stay out of sight and seems to play a teasing game. The poem shows close, affectionate observation of nature through a vivid simile.

check.q: In 'Three Questions', who was the most important person while the king was digging?
check.why: The hermit explains that while the king dug, he was the person the king was with, and helping him saved the king's life.

sections.h: Unit 2 — A Gift of Chappals and The Rebel
sections.md:
**A Gift of Chappals (retold).** Ravi and his cousin Meena, staying with their grandmother Paati, secretly feed a stray kitten milk in the backyard and name it 'Rukku Manni' after an aunt. A beggar arrives at the gate, his feet blistered by the hot road. Ravi, moved, quietly gives him a pair of chappals he finds by the door. Inside, Meena's music teacher is giving her a violin lesson. When the lesson ends, he cannot find his chappals — Ravi had given away the teacher's own! Paati is embarrassed, but instead of scolding harshly she brings out a pair of chappals that belonged to the children's late grandfather, Thatha, and gives them to the teacher, who accepts them gracefully.

**Themes:** compassion, the difference between kindness and carelessness, family warmth and gentle humour. **Character points:** Ravi — kind but impulsive; Paati — patient and generous; the music master — dignified.

**The Rebel (meaning).** The poem describes the rebel as someone who always does the opposite of everyone else: when others have long hair he cuts his short; when they keep pets he keeps none; when they praise something, he criticises it. The final twist is that **if everyone became a rebel, he would become conventional** — so rebellion simply means being different. The poet suggests rebels are useful because they make us question habits, but the tone is light and ironic.

check.q: Whose chappals did Ravi give to the beggar?
check.why: Ravi unknowingly handed over the visiting music master's chappals, so Paati later gave him Thatha's pair.

sections.h: Unit 3 — Gopal and the Hilsa Fish and The Shed
sections.md:
**Gopal and the Hilsa Fish (retold).** In a Bengal kingdom during the hilsa season, everyone talks of nothing but hilsa — buying, cooking, eating it. The irritated king challenges his witty courtier **Gopal**: buy a hilsa and bring it to the palace without anyone asking about it. Gopal appears next day half-shaved, smeared with ash, in torn clothes like a madman — carrying a hilsa. People in the market are so busy staring and commenting on his appearance that nobody mentions the fish. Even at the palace, people talk about his strange looks, not the hilsa. Gopal wins the reward, and the hilsa talk is broken.

**Themes:** wit, presence of mind, misdirection (like a magician drawing your eye elsewhere). Gopal Bhar is a famous figure of Bengali folk humour.

**The Shed (meaning).** A child is both scared and fascinated by an old garden shed with a creaky door, cobwebs and a dark window where the child imagines a face. An elder brother's teasing — that a man with big hands lives inside — feeds the fear. The child keeps promising to go in *one day*, but not yet. The poem captures childhood imagination, fear of the unknown, and the slow growth of courage.

check.q: How did Gopal make sure nobody asked about the hilsa?
options: He hid it in a basket
He disguised himself so strangely that people talked only about his looks
check.why: His half-shaved, ash-smeared appearance drew all attention away from the fish.

sections.h: Unit 4 — The Ashes That Made Trees Bloom and Chivvy
sections.md:
**The Ashes That Made Trees Bloom (retold).** A kind, childless old farmer and his wife love their little dog. One day the dog leads the farmer to a spot and digs; the farmer finds gold coins. Their greedy, mean neighbour borrows the dog, forces it to dig, finds only rubbish, and kills it. The heartbroken farmer buries the dog under a pine tree. The dog appears in a dream and tells him to cut the pine and make a mortar; rice pounded in it turns into gold. The neighbour borrows the mortar; for him the rice turns to filth, so he burns it. The dog appears again: the farmer gathers the ashes, which make withered cherry trees burst into bloom. He makes a dead cherry tree flower before the **daimyo** (feudal lord), who rewards him richly. The neighbour copies him, but his ashes fly into the lord's eyes and he is arrested and punished.

**Features:** folk tale structure, **rule of three** (gold, mortar, ashes), clear moral (kindness rewarded, greed punished).

**Chivvy (meaning).** 'Chivvy' means to nag or hurry someone. The poem is a list of adults' instructions to a child — don't talk with your mouth full, say please, don't stare, sit up straight, blow your nose. The last line tells the child to **think for themselves** — ironic, since every line before has told them exactly what to do. The poem gently questions how much freedom children are given.

check.q: What happened to the greedy neighbour at the end?
options: His ashes blew into the lord's eyes and he was punished
check.why: He tried to copy the farmer, but the ashes flew into the daimyo's eyes, and he was arrested for it.

sections.md:
**Quality (retold).** The narrator has known the **Gessler brothers**, German bootmakers in a small London shop, since his youth. They make boots only to order, by hand, of the finest leather; the boots last astonishingly long. The elder brother is passionate about his craft and bitter about big firms that win trade by advertisement rather than by work. Over the years, the narrator visits less often because his boots never wear out. Trade falls; half the shop is let to another business; the younger brother dies. The narrator finds the elder Gessler older and thinner each visit, yet the quality never drops. At last the narrator orders several pairs; when he returns, a young Englishman runs the shop and tells him Gessler has died — of **slow starvation**, because he worked day and night on boots, spent his money on the best leather and rent, and ate too little. Yet, the new owner admits, he made good boots.

**Themes:** dedication and integrity vs commercialism and advertising; the cost of refusing to compromise; tragedy. Gessler is tragic, not foolish — the world stopped valuing his kind of excellence. His broken English shows he is a foreigner in London.

**Trees (meaning).** A list poem on what trees are *for*: for birds to build nests, for children to climb, for shade, for sunsets to rest in, for leaves to whisper, for planting. The repeated 'Trees are…' builds a joyful catalogue reminding us how much trees give.

check.q: Why did Gessler lose his customers?
options: Big firms advertised and his boots lasted very long
check.why: His long-lasting boots meant few repeat orders, while advertised mass-made boots attracted buyers.

sections.h: Unit 6 — Expert Detectives and Mystery of the Talking Fan
sections.md:
**Expert Detectives (retold).** Told by young **Nishad (Nishu)**, this story follows him and his elder sister **Maya** as they wonder about **Mr Nath**, a lonely, unshaven man who lives alone and rarely speaks. Maya, inspired by detective stories, suspects he might be a criminal connected with a recent crime and keeps 'investigating'. Nishu, however, notices his kindness: Mr Nath was gentle and generous with him. Their mother explains Mr Nath's sad past — he had suffered great loss, and grief changed him. The children realise how wrong their suspicion was and resolve to be kind to him. The humour comes from the gap between Maya's dramatic 'detective' theories and the simple truth.

**Themes:** judging by appearances, prejudice, empathy, how loss affects people.

**Mystery of the Talking Fan (meaning).** A ceiling fan seems to 'talk' — it whirs and creaks as though chattering. The 'mystery' is solved at the end with a pun: it talks because it has **a screw loose** — both literally (a loose screw makes noise) and as the idiom for someone a bit crazy.

check.q: What lesson do Maya and Nishu learn in 'Expert Detectives'?
options: Never judge someone by their appearance
check.why: Mr Nath turns out to be a kind, grieving man, so the children learn not to judge by looks.

sections.h: Unit 7 — The Invention of Vita-Wonk and Dad and the Cat and the Tree
sections.md:
**The Invention of Vita-Wonk (retold, from Roald Dahl).** Mr **Willy Wonka**'s earlier invention, Wonka-Vite, made people younger — but Grandma Georgina took too much and became 'minus' (vanished below zero age). To bring her back, Wonka decides to invent the opposite: **Vita-Wonk**, which makes people older. He describes, with comic exaggeration, how he collected the oldest things on Earth and extracted their 'essence'. Grandma Georgina returns — but now impossibly old, far older than anyone has ever been. Dahl's style uses invented words, nonsense, lists and fast dialogue.

**Themes:** imagination, the dangers of excess, humour through exaggeration. Wonka is eccentric, confident, impatient and inventive.

**Dad and the Cat and the Tree (meaning).** The family cat is stuck up a tree. The family want to call the fire brigade, but **Dad** proudly insists he can rescue it. He climbs, slips and falls into the flowerbed; tries a ladder; tries jumping off the garage roof to grab a branch. The cat calmly jumps down by itself — and Dad is left stuck in the tree! Humour, sound words, a twist ending, and a mild lesson about pride and overconfidence.

check.q: What does Vita-Wonk do?
check.why: Vita-Wonk is the opposite of Wonka-Vite and adds years to a person's age.

sections.h: Unit 8 — Fire: Friend and Foe and Meadow Surprises
sections.md:
**Fire: Friend and Foe (summary).** This informative chapter explains how fire helped humans — cooking, warmth, light, protection from animals, metal-working, engines — and how it also destroys homes, forests and lives.

- **What fire needs** (the fire triangle): **fuel**, **heat** (enough to reach the burning temperature) and **oxygen**. Remove any one and fire goes out.
- **Water** cools burning material below its burning temperature, but **must not** be used on burning oil (it spreads the fire) or on electrical fires (danger of shock).
- **Carbon dioxide** and sand **smother** a fire by cutting off oxygen; fire extinguishers use this idea.
- **Firebreaks** — clearings in forests — remove fuel so a forest fire cannot spread.
- The **fire brigade** has hoses, ladders, protective suits and training; firefighters are brave public servants. In India, call 101.

**Meadow Surprises (meaning).** The poet invites us to look closely in a meadow to find hidden wonders: a butterfly sipping nectar, a rabbit hiding in the grass, a dandelion seed-head you can blow into the wind. The message is to walk gently and observe nature carefully and quietly.

check.q: Which side of the fire triangle does a firebreak remove?
check.why: A firebreak clears trees and grass, so the fire runs out of fuel.

sections.h: Unit 9 — A Bicycle in Good Repair and Garden Snake
sections.md:
**A Bicycle in Good Repair (retold, from Jerome K. Jerome).** The narrator plans a morning ride, but a friend arrives early, offers to 'help' and decides the bicycle needs adjusting. He removes the front wheel, loses the little ball-bearings, puts the wheel back so it wobbles, decides the gear-case needs work, then fights with the chain until things are far worse. By midday both men are tired, dirty and hurt, the bicycle is out of action, and the friend leaves cheerfully, sure he has done a good job. The humour comes from understatement, exaggeration and the friend's unshakeable confidence.

**Themes:** humour, overconfidence, 'don't fix what isn't broken', politeness that lets a guest cause trouble.

**Garden Snake (meaning).** The speaker is frightened on seeing a snake in the garden, but learns that it is a harmless garden snake that helps by eating pests. Fear changes to understanding. Pair this poem with *Expert Detectives* and *The Shed* for questions on fear and prejudice.

check.q: What is the main source of humour in 'A Bicycle in Good Repair'?
options: A friend who confidently 'repairs' a bicycle that was fine and ruins it
check.why: The comedy grows from the friend's unwanted, overconfident tinkering that leaves the bicycle worse.

sections.md:
**The Story of Cricket (summary).** Cricket grew from village games in England. Key points:

- The first written **Laws of Cricket** were drawn up in **1744**; the **Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC)** was founded in **1787** and became the guardian of the laws.
- Equipment changed: the bat went from **curved** (for balls bowled along the ground) to **straight** as bowlers began to pitch the ball; a third stump was added; pads and gloves came with faster bowling; the **helmet** appeared in the 1970s; vulcanised rubber made protective gear possible.
- In England, cricket reflected class: rich amateurs ('Gentlemen') and paid professionals ('Players').
- In India, the **Parsis** were the first community to take up the game, founding the Oriental Cricket Club in Bombay in **1848**. Tournaments organised by religious community (the Quadrangular, later **Pentangular**) were criticised for dividing people; the **Ranji Trophy**, a national championship by region, took their place.
- India played its first **Test match in 1932** and won the **World Cup in 1983**.
- Television and satellite broadcasting turned cricket into a commercial giant, and the centre of the cricket world shifted to South Asia.

**Exam tip:** link changes in equipment to changes in technology and in the way the game was played.

MCC founded

check.q: Which community in India first took up cricket?
check.why: The Parsis of Bombay began playing early and founded the Oriental Cricket Club in 1848.

sections.md:
Your supplementary reader has its own stories, often asked in short answers. Memory-jog retellings of the ones most often asked:

- **The Tiny Teacher** — an informative piece about **ants**: their colonies, the queen who lays eggs, workers who build, nurse young and gather food, soldiers who defend, and ants that 'milk' aphids for honeydew. Lesson: cooperation and hard work.
- **Bringing Up Kari** (Dhan Gopal Mukerji) — the narrator raises a baby elephant, Kari, who needs huge amounts of tender branches, once rescues a boy from drowning in a river, learns commands, and even learns to help himself to bananas from the table. Theme: the bond between a boy and an animal, and patient training.
- **Golu Grows a Nose** (based on Rudyard Kipling's 'Just So' story) — curious baby elephant Golu, whose nose was once short, keeps asking what the crocodile eats for dinner. He finds a crocodile, which grabs his nose and pulls; with a python's help he escapes — with a long trunk, which turns out to be wonderfully useful.
- **A Tiger in the House** (Ruskin Bond) — Grandfather brings home a tiger cub, Timothy, who grows up with a dog and a monkey; when he becomes too big and dangerous, he is sent to a zoo. Months later Grandfather visits and fondly strokes 'Timothy' — then learns Timothy had died, and this was a different, wild tiger!
- **The Bear Story** (Leo Tolstoy), **Chandni** and **An Alien Hand** — revise these directly from the textbook, noting the main characters, setting, problem and ending for each.

**Answer tip:** for any supplementary story, prepare four lines — who, where, what went wrong, how it ended — plus one theme.

check.q: In 'A Tiger in the House', what was surprising about Grandfather's zoo visit?
options: The tiger he stroked was not Timothy but a wild tiger
check.why: Timothy had died earlier, so the tiger Grandfather affectionately stroked was a different, wild one.
